SFNC.name: Simmons First National
SFNC.numbers_line: EPS $0.54 vs $0.535 est (in line); revenue $251M vs $254M est (light); NIM 3.92% (+8bp), period-end loans down meaningfully on paydowns and pricing discipline; ~$40M of one-time charges from the September restructuring.
SFNC.guidance: Full-year NII growth at the high end of 9–11%; expenses flat to slightly down versus the 2–3% growth guided in January; ~$40M of pre-tax revenue improvement from the initiatives, part reinvested in deposit gathering and C&I bankers; 26 branch closures; buybacks resume with 'increasing' appetite after a deliberate Q3 pause; three hikes modelled (December, March, June) with an 85% loan beta and a 30–35% deposit beta; deposit cost exit rate 1.83% is 'probably the bottom'. Investor day 10 December.
call_said: The quarter was a Q&A-only call and the message was about competition: 'we see risk spreads being competed away', brokered-deposit costs now ~30bp above FHLB advances because the whole system wants wholesale funding to fund loan growth, and the CEO is 'less optimistic about growth in the immediate term' (Q4 and Q1).

Paydowns were the largest in two-plus years: over $1B of $5M-plus payoffs carried under $50M of deposits, 'single-threaded' relationships Simmons let walk; new production earns a return on capital ~300bp above what ran off; $2.1B of sub-4% fixed loans remain to reprice or leave.

A consumer money-market test cut rates 15–20bp with almost no attrition and the $2M saved was recycled into promos, 75% of which brought new money; talent dislocation across the footprint is 'very, very ripe for harvest'.
SFNC.quote: "We see risk spreads being competed away." — Jay Brogdon
SFNC.read_through: The small-bank counterpoint to PNC and USB: the loan growth the big banks are booking is being chased at thin spreads, and wholesale funding is getting expensive as the system funds it. A regional read for the smaller banks in the universe (HWC tonight, CATY, FULT and CVBF this week).

TRV.name: Travelers
TRV.numbers_line: Core EPS $9.18 vs $7.39 est (large beat); revenue $12.4B vs $11.4B est; core ROE 22.1% (24.1% trailing); combined ratio 86.8%, underlying 84.1%; after-tax net investment income a record $908M (+7%); $1.5B of buybacks.
TRV.guidance: Fixed-income NII ~$875M after tax in Q4 and ~$3.3B for 2026; for 2027 'more than $3B' building from ~$875M in Q1 to ~$965M in Q4 as new money comes in ~120bp above portfolio yield. Expense ratio a little below 29% this year and about the same next. A larger cyber quota-share cession cuts net written premium by ~$165M in Q4 and ~$230M in 2027 with de minimis earnings impact. The ~$5.5B underlying underwriting-income 'zip code' is durable into 2027, give or take.
call_said: Pricing is softening in an orderly way: business-insurance renewal premium change 4.1% (7% ex property), retention 86%, the property decline 'very small' but 'not prepared to call the bottom'; personal auto renewal change slightly negative after ~10 rate decreases. Loss trend 'as we have expected… no surprises'.

The rate shock in insurance clothing: the after-tax unrealized investment loss widened from $2.0B to $6.4B in the quarter, 'interest rate driven not credit quality driven', held to maturity, no cash or statutory effect, and a tailwind to reinvestment. Reserve development was $234M favourable across all three segments despite a $295M asbestos charge.

AI in claims: a digital tool for unrepresented claimants with 80%-plus engagement, AI summarising hundred-page files against attorney demands, with the stated aim to 'bend the loss cost curve' on legal-system abuse; on AI shopping assistants (Muse) 'it is early days… the actual volume of observable activity is pretty minor'. Cyber book mostly at $1M limits or less and heavily reinsured.
TRV.quote: "The ZIP code that we are in now is just a completely different ZIP code than we used to be in." — Dan Frey, CFO
TRV.read_through: Carriers earn more on every dollar reinvested while pricing drifts lower, and the same rate move that hit bank AOCI hit insurers' unrealized losses. Read for CB (tonight), PGR (reported 14 Oct, no stored call) and ALL.

CLF.name: Cleveland-Cliffs
CLF.numbers_line: EPS $0.28 vs $0.21 est (beat); revenue $5.61B vs $5.69B est (light); adjusted EBITDA $612M vs $575M guided and more than double Q2's $286M; shipments 4.2Mt, average selling price $1,177/t (+$53), unit cost −$17/t.
CLF.guidance: Q4 adjusted EBITDA ~$715M with another $45–55/t of price; 2027 'realistically' more than $1B of EBITDA a quarter and over $4B for the year, the best since the 2021 record. The 2027 contract round: more than $1B of year-over-year EBITDA improvement before any index move, more than half signed, everything moving to index with lower discounts and take-or-pay minimums. Burns Harbor C-furnace reline pushed from mid-2027 to April 2028 (+500kt in 2027); capex ~$700M this year to just over $1B next; coal rolled over flat; leverage below 2–2.5× by mid-2027; no equity raise.
call_said: Goncalves on the market: the best price environment in three years, index pricing up ~$40/t every month, imports 35–40% below pre-Section-232 levels, customers 'more focused on securing volume than price', the Dearborn furnace stays idle until GM brings Chevy Trax production home from Korea and Ford puts steel back on the F-150.

Canada: TRQs fixed hot-rolled in four months but the Hamilton galvanizing line is idled with layoffs because Ottawa offered money instead of import limits; a long attack on Prime Minister Carney's trade trip and Chinese EV imports.

The USW contract has run past its deadline ('professional, respectful, and productive'); POSCO partnership talks continue; Middletown's $1B modernisation ($500M from the DOE) runs to Q1 2030; a 25% expansion of grain-oriented electrical steel at Butler for the grid; asset sales contracted to close in Q4, some delayed by power-supply and community issues.
CLF.quote: "Now the problem is no longer price. The problem is having access to steel." — Lourenco Goncalves
CLF.read_through: Steel pricing power is the input-cost headwind GM named the next morning (HRC at four-year highs, +50% y/y). Bullish for STLD (reported 19 Oct, no stored call) and NUE (26 Oct); the electrical-steel line is a quiet piece of the grid build-out.

GE.name: GE Aerospace
GE.numbers_line: EPS $2.25 vs $2.01 est (beat, +36%); revenue $14.1B vs $12.9B est (+18%); orders +49%, operating margin 22.5% (+220bp), free cash flow $2B. The stock was down ~4% at midday on a beat-and-raise.
GE.guidance: Raised across the board: revenue growth 19–20% (was high teens), operating profit $10.9–11.0B (+$300M), EPS $8.00–8.10 (+$0.30), free cash flow $9.1–9.4B (+$200M). 2027: commercial services growth 'low double digits' (from 'double digits'), defence high single digits, margins in line with 2026 as GE9X losses add ~$300M of headwind; CFM56 shop visits ~2,400, LEAP shop visits up ~25%. The 2028 cash target will be beaten in 2026.
call_said: The first question was about $111 Brent and airline profitability. Culp: departures grew 1% in Q3, schedules are being trimmed (Delta last Friday), but departures should still grow in 2027, the engine 'parking lot' awaiting shop visits is up 20% since January, and airlines are preparing for 'the other side'. CFM56 retirements are running at 1.5–2% against the 3–4% once expected.

Spare-parts delinquency rose again despite ten straight quarters of supplier input growth: demand is outrunning supply. 95% of Q4 revenue is already in backlog. Power-generation use of CFM56s (aeroderivatives) is a new spare-parts stream not in the 2028 guide.

Orders: IndiGo's 1,000-plus LEAP-1A deal (largest ever), Turkish Airlines 300 LEAP-1B, a $2.9B Navy F414 contract, the XA102 selected for the next NGAP phase, the F143 funded for JASSM, the CPP castings acquisition to add capacity 'for the entire aerospace industry'; GE9X mid-seal certification targeted by year-end.
GE.quote: "We will all get to the other side. There is no doubt about that." — Larry Culp
GE.read_through: Aerospace demand is intact and the beat-and-raise sold off anyway: oil at $111 is now an airline problem the market is pricing through the engine makers. Read for RTX (same morning), HON (22 Oct), BA (27 Oct) and UAL (tonight).

GM.name: General Motors
GM.numbers_line: EPS $3.70 vs $3.69 est (in line, +30% y/y); revenue a record $50.0B vs $48.8B est (+3%); EBIT-adjusted $4.1B (+22%), North America margin 8.7%, adjusted auto free cash flow $5.9B; a new $20B multi-year buyback. The stock was down ~8% at midday.
GM.guidance: Full-year EBIT-adjusted narrowed to $14.5–15.5B (midpoint unchanged), EPS to $12.75–13.75, auto free cash flow raised to $11.5–12.5B (from $9.5–11.5B), capex at the lower half of $10–12B. The commodity, logistics and DRAM headwind is now ~$2B for 2026, ~$400M worse since July. For 2027 GM 'continues to believe' it can grow revenue, margins and EBIT, but only if recent cost pressures moderate; annualising the inflation since July would be another $1–1.5B, 'roughly $2B' in total. Truck volumes flat in 2027 through the launch; guidance in January.
call_said: Barra: 'there are clear external headwinds, and in some cases, they are intensifying.' Copper at record prices and hot-rolled steel at four-year highs, both up 10–15% since July and ~50% versus last year's average; memory (DRAM) costs named as a line item; logistics surcharges hit within two to four weeks. 'We would need prices to come off of these levels a little bit' to grow in 2027.

The consumer: SAAR in the upper 16 millions, average transaction prices and trim mix strong, GM Financial delinquencies showing no shift; 'consumer sentiment surveys… have become disaggregated from consumer behavior on the ground'. Fuel prices may lift EV penetration; hybrids are coming in several segments with no extra capex.

The next-generation Silverado and Sierra are in production at Silao with Fort Wayne in Q1 and Orion in Q2; Super Cruise penetration in trucks to rise 4–5×, deferred software revenue approaching $7.5B; GM Defense growing 30%-plus; Level 3 highway driving on the 2028 Escalade IQ; Middle East sales redirected to the US.
GM.quote: "There are clear external headwinds, and in some cases, they are intensifying." — Mary Barra
GM.read_through: The first large consumer cyclical to say input inflation (copper, steel, memory) threatens 2027. That is the other side of CLF's and the memory makers' pricing power showing up in an end market. Read for F (22 Oct), TSLA (21 Oct) and the parts suppliers.
